job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Zoe Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the first finance hire at Tidewell, a 14-person startup in Bristol that sells reusable packaging to cafes. I do invoicing, expenses, a weekly cash report and whatever the founders throw at me, like pricing a new product at 4pm on a Friday. I use an AI assistant all day to draft emails and clean up spreadsheets. I live in a shared house with four people and a very loud cat, and my loan payments eat a good chunk of my salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a decent tool and a lot of hype around it, and that people get more out of it when they use it every day. In the pub I'd roll my eyes at anyone predicting the end of work. Online I'd post a few tips and the odd honest fail.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm fine with the plateau, because I've already got the benefit of the tools. My real worry is Tidewell. We've got about 14 months of cash, the founders are optimistic, and if the next round falls through I'm out on my ear with under a month of savings and a big loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep building little automations for the invoicing and the cash report and show the founders what I've saved. I'd start writing a weekly personal finance newsletter for people my age, which I've been wanting to do. I'd also quietly keep an eye on other finance jobs in Bristol, just in case Tidewell wobbles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good about AI, honestly. A bit wobbly about money, which I think is the normal state of being 22.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the money situation at Tidewell?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About 14 months at the current burn, and the founders say they're closing a round in the spring. I've seen the spreadsheet, which is a risk of being the finance person. I believe the founders 70 percent and I'm bracing for the other 30.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you spend the time the tools save?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use them on things nobody has time for, like customer pricing, where the money is. Last month I found we were undercharging one cafe chain by about 6 percent and that paid for my salary for a month. That's the sort of thing I want to do more of.

say: I'd say it's a decent tool with a lot of **hype** around it, and daily use is what helps.
Online I'd post a few **tips** and the odd honest fail.
think: I'm fine with the plateau, because I already get the **benefit** of the tools.
My real worry is **Tidewell**: 14 months of cash and a big loan on top.
do: Build more **automations** for invoicing and the cash report, and show the savings.
Start a weekly personal finance **newsletter** for people my age.
Quietly watch for other **finance jobs** in Bristol.
feel: Good about AI, and a bit **wobbly** about money, which feels normal at 22.

fieldNote: Her unease is about her **employer's** runway, not the technology.

steps.text: Automate the weekly cash report and invoicing
Start a weekly personal finance newsletter
Watch Bristol finance job listings in case Tidewell wobbles

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the real thing, that businesses like ours have a real edge if we use it well, and that the big bit of the work is learning what to ask. I'd also say that someone senior needs to explain to the team what's happening, not just announce it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm excited and also slightly threatened. Maybe 60 percent of my week could be done by a decent setup. If the founders realise that, they'd not need a second finance hire. But they'd also not need to hire an outside bookkeeper, and I might be the one who does the setting up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build a proper AI-supported finance setup for Tidewell, from invoicing to forecasts, and write down how it works so it's my project. I'd ask to be paid for the extra scope, even a small raise. I'd also take on two outside clients for the same kind of setup, charging 30 an hour for 8 hours a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Switched on. A bit like being on a surfboard when the wave arrives: thrilling but you do have to stay on the board.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much of your own job could the assistant do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, 60 percent, and it will grow. The parts that stay human are judging the founders' guesses, explaining numbers to a cafe owner and spotting when something odd is going on. I'd lean hard into those.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if Tidewell kept growing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to move from the finance role to an operations and finance role, so I'm involved in decisions and not only the reports. If the company doubled in size, I'd want to be the one who is running a small team, not the one who got replaced by a bigger team.

say: I'd say it's the **real thing**, and the big skill is learning what to ask.
I'd say someone senior should **explain** the change to the team, not just announce it.
think: Maybe **60 percent** of my week could be done by a decent setup, which feels exciting and threatening.
I might be the one who does the **setting up** instead of being replaced.
do: Build a proper **AI-supported** finance setup for Tidewell and document it.
Ask for a small **raise** for the extra scope.
Take two outside clients, **30** an hour for 8 hours a week.
feel: **Switched on**, like being on a surfboard when the wave arrives.

steps.text: Build and document an AI-supported finance setup for Tidewell

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're in a different world, and that anyone saying 'upskill' is selling something. I'd tell the founders we need to look at what Tidewell does that a machine can't copy, and fast. Online I'd probably go quiet for a bit, because I'd have no idea what to say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think I've got maybe 18 months of being useful and then nothing. Finance is thinking work, and a person who runs an assistant is not going to beat a thing that does the job on its own. I'd also guess startups like ours would fold or merge fast, because everyone's costs change at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut spending to the bone and push the newsletter hard to get a few hundred paying readers, because an audience might be the one thing that sticks. I'd try to land two or three recurring clients for the finance setups. And I'd look at jobs that involve physical or in-person stuff, like cafe management, where I know a lot of the owners.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Buzzing and nauseous at the same time. I'd be awake at 3am with the laptop open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do first, with two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, for about a year. It gets me ahead of the queue but the queue is going to disappear. What would protect me is trust, a name that people already believe. That's why I'd be pushing the newsletter and the client work now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does being good with the tools protect you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd write down a clear month by month plan, with numbers, because that's what I do. It would say: month one, cut costs; month two, ten clients; month six, break-even or move. It wouldn't be perfect but a plan stops me spiralling. It's the one thing I'm good at.

say: I'd say 'upskill' is what people say when they're **selling** something.
I'd ask the founders what Tidewell does that a machine **can't copy**.
think: I've got maybe **18 months** of being useful and then nothing.
Startups like ours might fold or **merge** fast when everyone's costs change at once.
do: Cut spending and push the **newsletter** to get a few hundred paying readers.
Land two or three **recurring clients** for finance setups.
Look at in-person work like **cafe management**, where I know owners.
feel: **Buzzing** and nauseous at once, awake at 3am with the laptop open.
S2.quote: I've got maybe 18 months of being useful and then nothing.
fieldNote: She is **honest** that AI skill only buys a head start before the queue vanishes.
Her plan leans on trust: an audience and recurring clients.
She calms herself with month-by-month plans, even imperfect ones.

steps.text: Cut spending to the bone for twelve months
Grow the newsletter to a few hundred paying readers
Write a month-by-month plan with money targets
Look at in-person cafe management roles

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is good enough to build something decent, and I'd say it to the founders and to my readers. I'd also say it's a chance to get ahead of everyone who's going to ignore this until it's too late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm optimistic. By 2031 I could have a small business, a few thousand readers and a loan that's nearly gone. The risk is that I think I'm cleverer than I am and miss the moment when the tools overtake me. I'd need someone to tell me when it's time to switch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the newsletter into a paid product and sell finance setups to small firms. I'd aim to earn 1000 a month from side work within two years, and use all of it to cut the loan. I'd also ask the Tidewell founders for equity, since I'd be building something that outlasts my salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Optimistic, with the occasional lurch. Like a good roller coaster: scary, but you chose to ride it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it either grows or gets absorbed. If it grows, I'd want a bigger role. If it's bought, I'd move quickly. I'd always keep the newsletter and the clients as my own, so that I'm not starting from zero.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to Tidewell in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably what I'd do is find a person, maybe an older accountant, who'd give me a straight opinion every six months. I don't want to rely only on how I feel, because that's what gets people stuck. A cheap outside view is worth more than I'd want to admit.

say: I'd say five years is good enough to **build** something decent.
I'd say it's a chance to get ahead of everyone who'll **ignore** it.
think: By 2031 I could have a small business and a loan that's **nearly gone**.
My risk is thinking I'm **cleverer** than I am and missing when the tools overtake me.
do: Grow the newsletter into a **paid** product and sell finance setups to small firms.
Aim for **1000** a month of side income within two years, and use it on the loan.
Ask the founders for **equity** in what I help build.
feel: **Optimistic**, like a good roller coaster that I chose to ride.
S3.quote: A cheap outside view is worth more than I'd want to admit.
fieldNote: Five years turns her curiosity into a **plan**: a paid newsletter and client work.
She names her own blind spot, overconfidence, and wants a mentor to check her.

steps.text: Turn the newsletter into a paid product
Put side income toward the student loan
Ask the Tidewell founders for equity
Find an older accountant for a six-monthly check-in

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time for most people to get ready if somebody tells them straight. I'd say we're lucky, and that being lucky is not a plan. I'd probably write a few newsletter issues about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm pretty relaxed. By 2036 I'll be 32, and I could have run a small firm of my own, paid off the loan and have a bit of equity. The only real danger is that I treat ten years as a long time and don't use the first two well, which is how I get stuck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work a couple more years at Tidewell or a similar firm, then go full-time on my own thing: finance setups plus the newsletter. I'd clear the loan in about five years and start investing 100 a month. I'd learn each new tool as soon as it appears, because it's easy when it's small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Light, almost. I'd still not take it for granted, but there's room to play and try things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years. What do you actually do with that much time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work on the dull bits first: clear the loan and build a three-month cushion. That makes everything else possible, because taking risks is easier when you aren't scared of the rent. Then I'd try the more ambitious things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a cousin who's 16?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say pick something you're curious about, learn how to use the new tools early, and don't borrow a fortune for a degree without checking what it leads to. And make something that's yours, even small. It teaches you more than a job does.

say: I'd say ten years is enough if somebody tells people **straight**.
I'd say being lucky is **not a plan**.
think: By 2036 I could be 32 with my own small firm, the loan paid and a bit of **equity**.
The danger is not using the **first two years** well, which is how I get stuck.
do: Work two more years at Tidewell, then go full-time on my own **firm** and newsletter.
Clear the loan in about **five** years and invest 100 a month.
Learn each new **tool** the moment it appears.
feel: **Light**, almost, with room to try things.
S4.quote: Taking risks is easier when you aren't scared of the rent.
fieldNote: With ten years she plans the **boring** steps first: loan and cushion.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I'm quick with the tools, but two years is not enough to clear a loan or build an audience, and I've got a startup that might not make it. What would help is some kind of income floor while people switch, a way to train that doesn't cost a fortune, and bosses who tell us what they see coming.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that people assume the ones who use AI every day are fine. We're fine until the thing we use gets better than we are, and then we're in exactly the same boat as everyone else, with less warning.

headlineQuote: We're fine until the thing we use gets better than we are, and then we're in exactly the same boat as everyone else, with less warning.
portrait: Zoe is a **22-year-old** finance hire at a Bristol startup, with a big loan, thin savings and a shaky employer.
She's centrist and adaptive, uses AI every day, and runs a side newsletter and small client jobs as her own safety net.
She trusts her own plans and numbers, but names her blind spot: thinking she's cleverer than she is.
Her mood is anxious mainly because of her startup's runway, and uneasy in most of the AI worlds.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** world, because it's too short to clear her loan or build an audience.
whatWouldHelp: An **income floor** while people switch, affordable training, and bosses who say early what they see coming.
